turns.user: why do recruiters spend only like 6 seconds on a resume? is that actually true
turns.assistant:
It comes from an eye-tracking study by a company called TheLadders in 2012, which found recruiters spent about 6 seconds on the first look. It's a real figure, but it was a small study, and it measured the initial screening scan, not the full review. A resume that passes that scan then gets read more carefully.

The reason it's quick is volume. A popular job posting can get hundreds of applicants, and recruiters need to filter fast to build a shortlist. So the first scan decides whether anyone reads further.

turns.user: so what are they looking at in those 6 secs
turns.assistant:
The eye-tracking showed they focus on a few spots: name, current title and company, previous title and company, dates, and education. They're checking whether your background matches the job.

That's why layout matters. Clear headings, consistent formatting, and job titles and dates that are easy to find help. Dense paragraphs and decorative designs make them harder to scan. Keywords from the job description also help, since the recruiter is matching quickly to the requirements.

turns.user: what about ats, does it actually reject you
turns.assistant:
Mostly no. Applicant tracking systems like Workday and Greenhouse parse your resume into fields and let recruiters search and filter. Few of them auto-reject on a score. The 'ATS rejects 75% of resumes' claim is mostly a myth.

What can happen is that bad formatting (tables, text in images, odd columns, headers/footers) causes the parser to misread your info, so you don't show up in searches. Also some employers set knockout questions (work authorization, required degree) that filter automatically. Use a clean single-column layout with standard headings and you'll be fine.

turns.user: why do they say one page for students
turns.assistant:
Because a student or new grad doesn't have enough experience to fill more than one page without padding, and recruiters are scanning quickly. One page forces you to include only your strongest items, which makes the scan easier.

It isn't a hard rule. Once you have several years of relevant experience, publications, or technical projects, a second page is fine. For a student, though, a second page often means including weak material that hides the good stuff.

turns.user: why do people get 221(g) after their visa interview. i had mine last week for f1 and the officer just gave me a white slip and kept my passport. am i rejected??
turns.assistant:
No, a 221(g) isn't a rejection. It's a temporary refusal under section 221(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which means the officer couldn't approve the visa on the spot and needs something more before deciding.

The white slip, usually called a blue, yellow or white slip depending on the case, tells you the reason. Common ones: administrative processing (extra security or background checks), missing documents, or a request for more information. If they kept your passport, it's typically because they plan to issue the visa after the follow-up is done.

turns.user: what did white slip mean tho, mine says administrative processing
turns.assistant:
That's the most common reason for an F-1 student. Administrative processing means your case is under additional review, often because of your field of study (certain technical fields are checked for export-control reasons under what's called Technology Alert List), your background, or sometimes a name match or random check. Most of these cases are cleared, but they take time.

The officer doesn't tell you the specific cause. It's usually a few weeks, but it can be a couple of months. You can't speed it up much, but you can check your status on the CEAC website and contact the consulate by email after a reasonable waiting time.

turns.user: how long do i wait before i email them
turns.assistant:
Wait at least 30 to 60 days from the interview, unless your program starts sooner, in which case you can write sooner and mention the start date. Many consulates say processing may take up to 180 days. Emailing earlier rarely changes the result and usually gets a template answer.

When you write, include your name, DS-160 confirmation number, passport number, interview date and a short note about your I-20 start date. Also tell your school's international office (DSO), who may be able to give you an updated start date or a deferral if you can't make it on time.

turns.user: ok and does this affect my chances of getting it eventually?
turns.assistant:
For most applicants, no. Administrative processing finishes with the visa being issued in the majority of cases. It's not a mark against you in itself, and you aren't banned from reapplying.

What can affect the outcome is answering any follow-up request quickly and accurately, such as sending the documents the slip asks for. If the slip asks for documents, upload or send them as instructed as soon as possible. Keep your I-20 and funds documents ready in case they're requested again.

turns.user: trying to pick between stronglifts 5x5, starting strength and gzclp. i'm 28, been lifting like 6 mo just random stuff, wanna do a real program. whihc is best
turns.assistant:
All three are linear progression programs for beginners, and they're similar:

- **Starting Strength**: 3 days a week, alternating A/B with squat each day, then bench or press, and deadlift or power clean. Very simple, minimal volume (3x5, one set of deadlift).
- **StrongLifts 5x5**: also 3 days A/B, squats every session, with 5 sets of 5 and barbell rows. More volume, has a popular app.
- **GZCLP**: 3 or 4 days, with tiers: heavy main lifts, then lighter volume work, then accessories. Better for slow progress as it gives you ways to deal with stalls.

For 6 months of random training, GZCLP or StrongLifts would be my pick.

turns.user: whats the diff between sl and gzclp when you stall
turns.assistant:
StrongLifts is simple when you stall: if you fail 5x5 at a weight three times in a row, you drop 10% and work back up. It's a single path with no flexibility. Once you stall a lot, usually after a few months, you're expected to move on.

GZCLP builds in the stall: when you fail to get all reps on a T1 lift (5x3+), it changes the rep scheme to 6x2, then 10x1, and then you reset with a lower weight. So it extends your linear progress for longer and also has T2 volume lifts and T3 accessories for arms, back and so on.

turns.user: is gzclp too complicated for first program
turns.assistant:
It's slightly more to keep track of, but it's not hard. You have a spreadsheet or an app (there's a free one on Reddit and several in the app store) that handles the numbers. The first couple of sessions feel confusing, but after a week it's routine.

StrongLifts is the easier one to start, with two workouts and one rule. If you like simplicity and want to get going now, choose that. If you want something that lasts longer and includes accessory work, choose GZCLP. Both will do the job.

turns.user: i only have 3 days tho
turns.assistant:
That works for either. For GZCLP, the standard layout is 4 days, but there's a 3-day version where you rotate 4 workouts (A1, B1, A2, B2) across the days, so each week the days shift. It's less symmetric, but it works well.

StrongLifts is built for 3 days a week, so there's no adaptation. Since you're limited to 3 days, StrongLifts is the more natural fit, and you can add a couple of accessories (curls, face pulls, calf raises) at the end if you have time.

Yes, that's the usual advice: start with just the 45 lb (20 kg) bar on bench, squat and rows (and 95 lb / 40 kg for deadlift), and add 5 lbs each session. Even if it feels too light, it lets you learn the movements and get used to the schedule while you build a habit.

turns.user: wanna start cooking vegan more, trying to decide between oat milk, soy milk and almond milk for cooking and coffee. which do u think is best
turns.assistant:
Depends on the use:

- **Soy milk**: closest to dairy milk in protein (about 7g per cup) and it behaves well when heated, so it's good for sauces, baking and custard. It can curdle in very hot coffee, though.
- **Oat milk**: creamy and sweet-ish, the best for coffee (barista editions foam well). It's a bit starchy in savory sauces.
- **Almond milk**: thin and low in calories and protein. Fine for smoothies and cereal but a weak choice for creamy dishes.

I'd get soy for cooking and oat for coffee, if you want one carton, barista oat.

turns.user: soy curdles in coffee? why
turns.assistant:
It's the combination of acidity and heat. Coffee is acidic, and when soy milk's proteins meet hot, acidic liquid they clump together. Cheaper soy milks with fewer stabilizers curdle more easily.

Tricks: let the coffee cool for a minute before adding it, pour the milk in first and then the coffee slowly, or use a barista soy milk, which has added stabilizers. Oat milk usually avoids this problem.

turns.user: what about for baking, cakes and stuff
turns.assistant:
For baking, soy milk is the safest choice because its protein helps with structure and browning. It also makes a good vegan buttermilk: add a tablespoon of lemon juice or vinegar to a cup of soy milk, wait 5 minutes, and it curdles into something that works with baking soda.

Oat milk also works in cakes and muffins, with a slightly softer result. Almond milk is okay, but you may notice a paler, less rich cake. Use unsweetened versions for savory dishes and baking where you control the sugar.

turns.user: is homemade worth it or just buy
turns.assistant:
For soy and oat, buying is usually easier and the store-bought has added calcium and B12. Homemade oat milk is quick (blend oats with cold water for 30 seconds, strain) but can turn slimy if you blend too long or use warm water, and it doesn't keep long, about 3 to 4 days.

Homemade soy milk is fresher and tastes great, but it takes a bit more work: soaking, blending, and boiling beans. It's worth trying if you drink a lot, and cheaper per litre. For occasional use, buying is more convenient.
